items.title: L9: Present value, effective rates and loan costs
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Financial questions at this level ask you to compare sums at different dates. Money received later is worth less than money now, because it could be invested or eroded by inflation. To find the present value of a future sum, divide by the growth multiplier for each year: £10,000 due in two years at a 3% discount rate is worth 10,000 ÷ 1.03² = £9,426 today. A series of payments is valued by discounting each one separately and adding them. The effective annual rate matters when interest is added more than once a year: 8% a year added quarterly means 2% each quarter, so the annual multiplier is 1.02⁴ = 1.0824, an effective rate of 8.24%, higher than 8%. Loans can be repaid in different ways. If the capital is repaid in equal parts and interest is charged on the opening balance each year, interest falls as the balance falls: £12,000 over four years at 5% costs interest of 600 + 450 + 300 + 150. Regular savings are valued by growing each deposit for the time it remains invested. To keep buying power constant when prices rise, multiply by the inflation multiplier for each year. Take care to say whether payments fall at the start or the end of each year, since that changes the number of years each is discounted or grown. Work to enough decimal places that rounding does not change the answer, and round at the end.

questions.prompt: Option A pays £9,500 now. Option B pays £10,000 in two years. Using a 3% annual discount rate, which is worth more today, and by roughly how much?

options.text: Option B, by about £209
Option A, by about £74
Option B, by £500
Option A, by £500

questions.hint: B's present value is 10,000 ÷ 1.0609 = £9,426, which is £74 less than £9,500.

questions.prompt: A savings account pays 8% a year with interest added quarterly at one quarter of the annual rate. What is the effective annual rate?
£12,000 is borrowed and repaid in four equal yearly capital payments, with 5% interest charged each year on the balance at the start of that year. What is the total repaid?
A salary of £40,000 must keep its buying power over five years while prices rise by 3% a year. What salary is needed after five years, to the nearest pound?
A fund pays £2,000 at the end of each of three years. Using a 4% discount rate, what is the present value of the payments, to the nearest pound?
£10,000 is invested for five years, either at 3.6% simple interest or at 3.3% interest compounded annually. Which gives more interest, and by roughly how much?

options.text: Simple interest, by about £180
Compound interest, by about £180
Compound interest, by about £37
Simple interest, by about £37

questions.hint: Simple earns £1,800 and compound earns about £1,763.

questions.prompt: A coat costing £80 is reduced by 20%. A further 10% is then taken off the sale price, and a £5 voucher is used. What is the final price?
£1,000 is paid into an account at the start of each of three years, earning 5% compound a year. What is the total at the end of the third year?

items.title: L9: Tolerances, bounds and margins of error
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Real data is measured, rounded or sampled, so exact answers are not always possible. A value rounded to a given accuracy lies in a range: 4.5 m to the nearest 0.1 m means at least 4.45 and less than 4.55. The upper bound is not reached exactly, but is used as the limit. When you add rounded numbers, add the lower bounds for the smallest possible total and the upper bounds for the largest. Three figures each rounded to the nearest £1,000 and reported as £12,000, £8,000 and £15,000 have a largest possible total of just under £36,500. Percentage error compares the difference with a base: a cost of £54,000 against a £48,000 estimate is 6,000 ÷ 48,000 = 12.5% over the estimate, but 11.1% of the actual. A tolerance is the permitted variation: a part 250 mm ±2% lies between 245 and 255 mm, and two such parts joined could be as short as 490 mm. A margin of error for a poll gives the range in which the true figure is likely to lie: 52% ±3 points means true support could be 49% to 55%, so a majority is not certain. Percent comparisons are not symmetrical: if B is 50% higher than A, A is only 33.3% lower than B. Enforcement margins may combine a percentage and a fixed amount.

questions.prompt: A length is given as 4.5 m, correct to the nearest 0.1 m. Which range contains the true length?

options.text: Between 4.5 m and 4.6 m
Between 4.4 m and 4.5 m
At least 4.40 m and less than 4.60 m
At least 4.45 m and less than 4.55 m

questions.hint: Rounding to 0.1 means up to 0.05 either way.

questions.prompt: A project was estimated at £48,000 and cost £54,000. By what percentage did the actual cost exceed the estimate?
Two items cost £12.50 and £7.30, each rounded to the nearest 10p. What is the largest total they could cost together, to the limit of the bounds?
questions.hint: The upper bounds are 12.55 and 7.35.

questions.prompt: A poll reports 52% support for a proposal, with a margin of error of ±3 percentage points. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: A majority supports the proposal, since 52% is over 50%
Support is exactly 52% among all adults
Support could be as low as 49%, so a majority is not certain
Three per cent of respondents were unsure

questions.hint: The range is 49% to 55%.

questions.prompt: Three budget figures are each rounded to the nearest £1,000 and reported as £12,000, £8,000 and £15,000. What is the largest the true total could be, to the limit of the bounds?
questions.hint: The upper bounds add to 12,500 + 8,500 + 15,500.

questions.prompt: A rod has a nominal length of 250 mm with a tolerance of ±2%. Two rods are joined end to end. What is the shortest combined length?

options.text: 495 mm
490 mm
480 mm
498 mm

questions.hint: 2% of 250 is 5, so each is at least 245 mm.

questions.prompt: Region B's rate is 50% higher than Region A's rate. By what percentage is A's rate lower than B's?
questions.hint: If A is 100 and B is 150, A is 50 below 150, which is a third.

questions.prompt: A speed camera is set to trigger only above the limit plus 10% plus 2 mph. What is the trigger speed in a 30 mph zone?

options.text: Above 35 mph
Above 36 mph
Above 33 mph
Above 32 mph

items.title: L9: Index numbers, weights and chained change
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Index numbers express a quantity relative to a base year set at 100. A reading of 132 means 32% above the base year. If the index moved from 80 to 100, the rise is 20 points on a base of 80, which is 25%. To rebase, divide each value by the new base value and multiply by 100: with 2018 = 100, 2020 = 110 and 2023 = 132, rebasing to 2020 gives 132 ÷ 110 × 100 = 120. A weighted index combines components using weights that add to 100%. If food (40%) rises 5%, energy (25%) rises 20% and housing (35%) rises 2%, the overall rise is 0.4 × 5 + 0.25 × 20 + 0.35 × 2 = 7.7%. A component's contribution is its weight times its change, and its share of the overall change is that contribution divided by the total. To chain changes, multiply the relatives: 1.04 × 1.06 = 1.1024, a rise of 10.2%. Real values remove the effect of price changes: divide the nominal index by the price index and multiply by 100, so a nominal 150 with prices at 125 gives a real 120. A falling rate of change is not a fall in the level: if inflation drops from 4.5% to 3.9%, prices still rise, only more slowly, and the gap is 0.6 percentage points.

questions.prompt: A price index has three components: food (weight 40%) rose 5%, energy (25%) rose 20% and housing (35%) rose 2%. What was the overall rise?
An index with 2018 = 100 reads 110 in 2020 and 132 in 2023. What is the 2023 value if the index is rebased so that 2020 = 100?
The 2022 index was 104 relative to 2021, and the 2023 index was 106 relative to 2022. What is the percentage rise from 2021 to 2023, to one decimal place?
Nominal spending has an index of 150 in 2024 (2019 = 100), and prices have an index of 125. What is the real spending index?
An index rises from 80 to 100. What is the percentage rise?
questions.hint: The rise is 20 on a starting value of 80.

questions.prompt: Component A (weight 30%) rose by 10% and component B (weight 70%) rose by 5%. What share of the overall rise came from A, to the nearest whole number?
questions.hint: A contributed 3 of the 6.5 points.

questions.prompt: Quarterly index values for a year are 100, 102, 105 and 103. The previous year's average was 98. By roughly what percentage did the annual average rise?
questions.hint: The average is 102.5, and 4.5 ÷ 98 is 4.6%.

questions.prompt: Inflation was 4.5% last month and is 3.9% this month. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Prices are falling, because inflation has fallen
Prices are rising at only 0.6%
Prices are still rising, but more slowly
Prices are falling by 0.6%

questions.hint: A fall in inflation is a fall in the rate of increase.

items.title: L9: Funnels, capacity and throughput
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Workflow questions track how many people or cases survive each stage and whether capacity matches demand. For a recruitment funnel, multiply the numbers by each stage's pass rate in order: 2,500 applications, 35% through the sift, 40% of those at assessment, 70% passing and 60% accepting leaves 2,500 × 0.35 × 0.4 × 0.7 × 0.6 = 147. To work backwards from a target, divide by each rate, not add percentages: to get 36 starters when 75% accept, 60% of those assessed pass and 80% of those invited attend, invite 36 ÷ (0.75 × 0.6 × 0.8) = 100 people. Capacity is staff × hours × days, and utilisation is demand divided by capacity. If capacity falls, find the shortfall in hours. Full-time equivalent counts people in proportion to their hours: a person on 60% of full-time hours is 0.6 FTE. Backlogs clear at the net rate, which is the rate of completion minus the rate of arrival. A process with several stages can only be right first time if every stage is right, so multiply the success rates. Seasonal demand varies around an average: 30% above and 20% below an average of 1,500 means 1,950 and 1,200. To staff a queue, convert calls per hour and minutes per call into workload hours, then allow for the occupancy you can sustain, usually below 100%.

questions.prompt: A campaign receives 2,500 applications. 35% pass the sift, 40% of those attend assessment, 70% of those pass, and 60% of those who pass accept an offer. How many join?
A team needs 36 new starters. 75% of offers are accepted, 60% of those who attend assessment are offered a post, and 80% of those invited attend. How many people should be invited?
A team of 12 staff each work 7 productive hours a day for 5 days, a total of 420 hours. A quarter of that capacity is lost to leave, and the week's work needs 336 hours. What is the shortfall?

options.text: None, because there are enough hours
21 hours
105 hours
84 hours

questions.hint: Capacity falls to 315 hours, and 336 − 315 = 21.

questions.prompt: A team has 5 full-time staff, 3 staff working 60% of full-time hours and 2 staff working 50%. What is the team's full-time equivalent?
A backlog of 1,200 cases builds up. 400 new cases arrive each week and 450 are completed. How many weeks will it take to clear the backlog?
questions.hint: The net clearance is 50 a week, and 1,200 ÷ 50 = 24.

questions.prompt: A letter passes through three stages. 4% have errors at the checking stage, 5% are rejected at approval and 2% fail at dispatch. What percentage get through all three stages correctly, to one decimal place?
A service averages 1,500 cases a month. December is 30% above the average and August is 20% below. How many more cases are expected in December than in August?
A helpline expects 70 calls in the busiest hour, and each call takes 6 minutes. Advisers can be busy no more than 85% of the time. How many advisers are needed?
questions.hint: The workload is 7 adviser-hours, and 7 ÷ 0.85 is 8.2, so 9.

items.title: L9: Risk, probability and false alarms
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Risk questions combine probabilities with consequences. The expected value of a risk is probability multiplied by impact, and several risks add: a 4% chance of a £250,000 loss and a 10% chance of a £40,000 loss give an expected loss of 10,000 + 4,000 = £14,000. For independent events, the chance that all happen is the product, and the chance that at least one happens is 1 minus the chance that none do. Two backups that fail 10% and 5% of the time both fail only 0.5% of the time, so at least one works 99.5% of the time. Screening is subject to false alarms. If 5% of 1,000 cases are fraudulent, a test that detects 90% of fraud and wrongly flags 10% of genuine cases flags 45 true and 95 false cases, so only 45 out of 140 flagged, about 32%, are fraudulent. A highly accurate test can therefore produce many false positives when the thing being tested for is rare. Relative and absolute risk differ: a fall from 4% to 3% is a 25% relative reduction but only 1 percentage point in absolute terms, so 100 people must be treated to avoid one case. For repeated trials, count the ways: the probability of exactly one failure in three checks that each fail with probability 0.1 is 3 × 0.1 × 0.9². Without replacement, probabilities change at each draw.

questions.prompt: In a group of 1,000 cases, 5% are fraudulent. A test detects 90% of fraud and wrongly flags 10% of genuine cases. What proportion of flagged cases are actually fraudulent, to the nearest whole per cent?
questions.hint: 45 of the 140 flagged cases are fraudulent.

questions.prompt: A project has a 4% chance of a £250,000 loss and a 10% chance of a £40,000 loss. What is the expected total loss?
Two independent systems fail with probabilities of 0.10 and 0.05 respectively. What is the probability that at least one of them works?
questions.hint: Both fail with probability 0.10 × 0.05 = 0.005.

questions.prompt: A department has 200 staff, of whom 120 are women. 90 of the women and 40 of the 80 men work part-time. A part-time worker is picked at random. What is the probability that the person is a woman, to the nearest whole per cent?
questions.hint: 90 of the 130 part-timers are women.

questions.prompt: Two names are drawn at random without replacement from 10 applicants, of whom 4 are internal. What is the probability that both are internal?
A treatment cuts the risk of an outcome from 4% to 3%. How many people need the treatment to prevent one outcome?
questions.hint: The absolute reduction is 1 percentage point.

questions.prompt: Preparing a bid costs £12,000. There is a 25% chance of winning a contract worth £70,000 in profit before bid costs. What is the expected net gain from bidding?

options.text: A loss of £12,000

questions.prompt: Three independent checks each fail with probability 0.1. What is the probability that exactly one of them fails?

items.title: L9: Verdicts in extracts with statistics and caveats
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Extracts from reports often include subgroups, definitions and caveats that change what can be concluded. Break the passage into groups and check that the statement refers to the right one. If 21 of 30 pilots succeeded and the 12 northern pilots had 6 successes, then outside the north 15 of 18 succeeded, so you can compare rates by subtracting. A rule that says approval is needed above a threshold does not tell you whether other grants also received approval. An 'average over the period' may be weighted if sample sizes differ, so a simple mean of annual figures may not be the figure the agency used. When a statement concerns a rate per person, compare the growth of the numerator and the denominator: complaints up 40% against staff up 20% means the rate rose. Be careful with timing words: if people sat a test 'within six months', some may have passed after the year ended. A policy may apply to defined conditions, such as leaving within two years of moving with exceptions for redundancy and ill health. Combine subgroup shares with weights: 35% of responses with an 80% rate plus 65% with a 40% rate gives 54% overall. Finally, notice when a figure is defined differently from the one in the statement, for example a survey's broad definition of bullying compared with a policy definition. If the definitions differ, you generally cannot transfer the figure.

questions.prompt: "A review of 30 pilot schemes found that 21 reduced processing times. Schemes in the north, 12 of the 30, were the least successful, with only 6 of the 12 reducing processing times." Statement: "Schemes outside the north were more likely to reduce processing times than schemes in the north." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the passage does not say where the other schemes were
True: 15 of 18 other schemes succeeded, against 6 of 12 in the north
Cannot say: the passage does not explain why some schemes failed
False: 21 of the 30 schemes succeeded overall

questions.hint: 21 − 6 = 15 successes outside the north, from 30 − 12 = 18 schemes.

questions.prompt: "A grant of over £250,000 requires ministerial approval. A department approved 14 grants last year. Three exceeded £250,000, and each of those received ministerial approval." Statement: "Grants under £250,000 never received ministerial approval." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the rule sets a requirement, not a ban on other approvals
Cannot say: the passage does not give the total value of the grants
True: only the three large grants needed ministerial approval
False: all 14 grants were approved by the minister

questions.hint: A requirement above a threshold does not forbid approval below it.

questions.prompt: "An agency's satisfaction score was 78% in 2021, 81% in 2022 and 79% in 2023. The agency says its 80% target was met on average over the period." Statement: "The agency's statement is accurate." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: the score in 2022 was above 80%
False: the simple average of the three scores is below 80%
Cannot say: the passage does not say how satisfaction was measured
Cannot say: respondent numbers are not given, so the average may be weighted

questions.hint: An average weighted towards the 81% year could reach 80%.

questions.prompt: "Over five years a unit's headcount rose from 180 to 216, and complaints rose from 90 to 126." Statement: "Complaints per member of staff rose over the five years." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: it is not known whether staff caused the complaints
Cannot say: the figures for the years in between are not given
True: complaints rose by 40% while headcount rose by 20%
False: headcount also rose

questions.prompt: "A licence needs a written test and a practical test. In 2023, 1,000 people sat the written test and 70% passed. Of those who passed, 80% sat the practical test within six months, and 90% of those passed it." Statement: "More than 500 people obtained the licence in 2023." Which option is correct?

options.text: False: only 70% passed the written test
Cannot say: passing both tests might not mean a licence is issued
Cannot say: some of the practical tests may have taken place after 2023
True: 504 people passed both tests

questions.hint: The six-month window runs beyond the end of the year.

questions.prompt: "Employees may be required to repay relocation costs if they leave within two years of moving, unless they leave through redundancy or ill health. Carlos moved in March 2022 and resigned in January 2024 to take another job." Statement: "Carlos may be required to repay his relocation costs." Which option is correct?

options.text: True: he left within two years and neither exception applies
False: he left more than two years after the move
Cannot say: it is not known whether he moved voluntarily
Cannot say: the amount he received is not stated

questions.hint: March 2022 to January 2024 is 22 months.

questions.prompt: "In a consultation, 35% of responses came from organisations and 65% from individuals. Of the organisations' responses, 80% opposed the proposal. Of the individuals' responses, 40% opposed it." Statement: "A majority of all responses opposed the proposal." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: the total number of responses is not given
True: opposition was 28% plus 26%, which is 54% of all responses
Cannot say: the number of organisations is not given
False: most responses came from individuals, who mostly supported it

questions.prompt: "A report found that around one in five staff had experienced bullying, using a definition broader than the one in the department's policy." Statement: "One in five staff have experienced conduct that breaches the department's bullying policy." Which option is correct?

options.text: Cannot say: 'around one in five' is too vague to use
False: the report's definition is wider than the policy's, so fewer breached it
True: one in five is the figure the report gives
Cannot say: the report used a broader definition than the policy

questions.hint: A figure based on one definition cannot be assumed for another.

items.title: L9: Weighing the strength of arguments
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Some questions ask which argument is strongest or weakest on an issue. A strong argument is relevant to the question, specific, supported by evidence or a clear mechanism, and important enough to matter. A weak argument is vague, relies on assertion or popularity, appeals to feelings alone, or concerns something minor. When choosing the strongest argument for a proposal, look for the one that addresses its main purpose: pilot results showing faster casework with no extra errors speak directly to a proposal for a portal. When choosing the strongest argument against, look for a serious consequence that is likely and not easily avoided: excluding people who are entitled to a service is more serious than inconvenience. Distinguish how likely an effect is from how large it would be, and whether the argument deals with the proposal as stated. Arguments that merely restate the proposal, appeal to novelty, or note that others do the same are weak. Be wary of arguments that rely on a possibility with no evidence of likelihood, or that apply to every option equally. Worked example: for a proposal to keep a paper application route, the argument that some claimants lack internet access and would be blocked from claiming is strong because it is relevant and consequential. The argument that paper is traditional is weak.

questions.prompt: Proposal: move all routine casework to an online portal. Which is the strongest argument in favour?

options.text: Staff would enjoy learning a new piece of software and using it daily
Pilot sites cleared cases 30% faster with no rise in errors
Online portals are more modern than paper-based systems
Many other organisations already use online portals for casework

questions.hint: It gives specific evidence about the main purpose of the change.

questions.prompt: Proposal: require a photo ID check for a service. Which is the strongest argument against?

options.text: Some people would find showing ID a nuisance when they apply
A similar system once took a long time to build
The check would add a few seconds to each application
Entitled people without ID would be excluded, with no other route

questions.hint: It identifies a serious likely harm to the service's purpose.

questions.prompt: Proposal: make a training course compulsory for all staff. Which is the weakest argument in favour?

options.text: Records of attendance would show which staff may need extra support
The course is a legal requirement for some roles
Training is a good thing, and good things should be compulsory
Staff who did the course made fewer errors in a trial

questions.hint: It asserts the conclusion and does not use evidence about this course.

questions.prompt: Proposal: keep a paper route alongside the online application form. Which is the strongest argument in favour?

options.text: Some claimants have no internet access and could not otherwise claim
Some staff prefer to process paper applications at their desks
Paper forms look more official than online ones
Paper forms have been used for many years

questions.hint: It identifies a consequence that matters for the service's purpose.

questions.prompt: Proposal: extend helpline opening hours to 8pm on weekdays. Which is the strongest argument in favour?

options.text: Some other helplines already open until 8pm on weekdays
Data show 20% of callers ring after 5pm and abandon the closed line
Longer opening hours would sound more helpful to the public
Staff would be paid overtime for the extra hours

questions.hint: It shows evidence of unmet demand.

questions.prompt: Proposal: merge two small teams into one. Which is the strongest argument against?

options.text: Both teams hold specialist knowledge, and a trial merger lost half of it
Some people prefer to work in smaller groups than larger ones
The merged team would need a new name and logo
Staff may find it unsettling to work with new colleagues

questions.hint: It gives specific evidence of a serious loss that the merger would risk.

questions.prompt: Proposal: publish monthly performance data on the department's website. Which is the weakest argument against?

options.text: Smaller teams could be identified from the figures
Poorly explained data could be misread, and no context is planned
Publishing data takes effort, and effort is tiring
The department cannot yet produce reliable monthly figures

questions.hint: It is trivial compared with the other objections, none of which deal with the proposal's content.

questions.prompt: Proposal: replace a long paper guidance manual with a short online summary. Which is the strongest argument in favour?

options.text: The manual is currently kept in a cupboard on the third floor
Many staff do not read the manual at all
Short documents are better than long ones
In a trial, staff found answers in half the time with no more errors

questions.hint: It compares speed and accuracy directly.

items.title: L9: Reasoning with most, few, some and at least
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Quantifiers such as 'most', 'few', 'at least' and 'more than' follow rules that can be used to deduce things safely. If more than half of a group has one property and more than half has another, then at least one member has both, because the two majorities must overlap. More generally, if one group is more than 70% of the total and another is more than 40%, the overlap must be at least 70 + 40 − 100 = 10%. The same method works in reverse: if a group is more than 50% of the whole and another is at least 66.7%, they overlap by at least 16.7%. Fractions chain by multiplication: if at least three quarters of cases close within 30 days and at least two thirds of those close within 14, then at least half of all cases close within 14 days. 'All A are B' and 'No B are C' together mean that no A are C. 'Some' means at least one and does not exclude 'all'. A conclusion about 'most' of a subgroup does not follow just because the whole group has a majority, because the overlap may be a small share of the subgroup. Be careful not to conclude that a negative is true because it was not stated. Test each option by looking for an arrangement of numbers that satisfies the premises but breaks the option, and if you find one, the option is not forced.

questions.prompt: Most claims are processed within 5 days. Most claims are submitted online. Which statement must be true?

options.text: At least one claim was both submitted online and processed within 5 days
Most online claims are processed within 5 days
Few paper claims are processed within 5 days
All claims processed within 5 days were submitted online

questions.hint: Two majorities of the same group must overlap.

questions.prompt: More than 70% of staff work mainly in an office, and more than 40% of staff work part-time. Which statement must be true?

options.text: More than 40% of office staff work part-time
Part-time staff never work from home
Most part-time staff work mainly in an office
More than 10% of staff both work mainly in an office and work part-time

questions.hint: 70 + 40 − 100 = 10, so the overlap is above 10%.

questions.prompt: All inspectors are trained. Some trained staff are not inspectors. No trainee is trained. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Some inspectors are trainees
Nobody who is a trainee is an inspector
Some trainees are trained staff
All trained staff are inspectors

questions.hint: Inspectors are trained, and trainees are not.

questions.prompt: Every report was either approved or returned. Some returned reports were resubmitted. All resubmitted reports were approved. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Some approved reports were never returned
All returned reports were resubmitted
Some reports were returned and later approved
Reports were never returned more than once

questions.hint: The resubmitted reports were returned and then approved.

questions.prompt: At least three quarters of cases are closed within 30 days. Of the cases closed within 30 days, at least two thirds are closed within 14 days. Which statement must be true?

options.text: At least one third of cases are closed within 14 days
At least two thirds of all cases are closed within 14 days
At least half of all cases are closed within 14 days
At least three quarters of cases are closed within 14 days

questions.prompt: More than half of survey respondents are over 40, and fewer than a third of respondents are women. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Most men are over 40
Most women are under 40
At least one woman is over 40
At least one man is over 40

questions.hint: Men are more than two thirds, and the over-40s are more than a half, so they overlap.

questions.prompt: Some new starters have degrees. Every new starter completes induction. No one who completes induction leaves in the first month. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Nobody among the new starters with a degree leaves in the first month
Some new starters leave in the first month
Induction is completed only by graduates
All new starters have degrees

questions.hint: All starters complete induction, so none leave in the first month.

questions.prompt: All grade 7 staff who applied were interviewed. Nobody interviewed was turned down without feedback. Which statement must be true?

options.text: Some grade 7 applicants were turned down
Every grade 7 applicant who was turned down got feedback
All applicants were interviewed
Feedback was given to every applicant

questions.hint: Grade 7 applicants were interviewed, and interviewees got feedback if turned down.

items.title: L9: Statistical flaws in policy arguments
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Policy arguments often use statistics in ways that mislead. Recognising the pattern lets you spot the flaw quickly. Numbers versus rates: a rise in the number of incidents may only reflect a rise in the number of people at risk, so compare rates. Selection effects: comparing only those who completed or survived a programme excludes those who dropped out, who may differ. No comparison group: a high success rate means little without knowing what would have happened otherwise, especially if participants chose to take part. Case mix: a higher death rate at one hospital may reflect that it treats more severe cases. Random variation: one unusually low month does not show a lasting change. Percentage points: a fall in the unemployment rate from 5.0% to 4.5% is half a percentage point, not half a per cent, and the rate fell by 10%. Base rates: if a condition is rare, even an accurate test will produce more false alarms than true cases. Cherry-picking: interviewing only successful teams cannot show what makes teams successful, because unsuccessful teams may do the same things. Worked example: 'The number of accidents involving drivers over 70 has doubled, so older drivers are more dangerous.' The flaw is that the number of older drivers may also have grown, so the rate per driver may not have risen. Always ask what comparison is missing.

questions.prompt: "The number of road accidents involving drivers over 70 has doubled in ten years, so older drivers have become more dangerous." What is the main flaw?

options.text: It compares ten years, which is too short a period
It compares numbers, not rates, and older drivers may have grown in number
It assumes older drivers drive more slowly than younger drivers do
It does not say how severe the accidents were

questions.hint: A doubling in numbers could reflect a doubling in the population at risk.

questions.prompt: "Of 200 businesses that used our advice service, 90% were still trading after five years, so the service keeps businesses alive." What is the main flaw?

options.text: There is no comparison with similar businesses that did not use the service
Five years is too short a period to judge survival properly
It does not give the cost of the service
The figure of 90% is too high to be correct

questions.hint: Businesses that seek advice may be more likely to survive in any case.

questions.prompt: "Our prison education programme works: only 15% of those who completed it reoffended." What is the main flaw?

options.text: It assumes that education cannot reduce reoffending
It uses a percentage and not the number of people
It ignores those who dropped out, who may differ from those who finished
It does not say what the reoffending rate is for the general population

questions.hint: Counting only completers excludes the least successful.

questions.prompt: "Hospital A has a higher death rate than Hospital B, so Hospital A provides worse care." What is the main flaw?

options.text: Death rates are not a proper measure of hospital quality
It does not give the cost of care at each hospital
It does not say how many beds each hospital has
It does not allow for Hospital A treating more severe cases

questions.hint: Patients' conditions may differ between hospitals.

questions.prompt: "This month's complaints, at 12, are the lowest ever recorded, so the new policy has worked." What is the main flaw?

options.text: Complaints are not the best single measure of service quality
A single low month may just be random variation
The number 12 is too small to be reliable
The policy was introduced only recently

questions.hint: One data point cannot show a trend.

questions.prompt: "Unemployment fell from 5.0% to 4.5%, a fall of 0.5%, so the number of unemployed people fell by only half of one per cent." What is the main flaw?

options.text: It confuses 0.5 percentage points with 0.5 per cent, as the rate fell by 10%
It assumes the number of unemployed people is fixed
It ignores the effect of people leaving the labour force
It uses rounded figures that could be inaccurate

questions.prompt: "The test is 95% accurate, so if it flags a case as fraudulent, there is a 95% chance that the case is fraudulent." What is the main flaw?

options.text: It assumes all cases are tested in exactly the same way
It assumes that a test cannot be wrong
It fails to say how much the test costs
It ignores how rare fraud is, since most flagged cases may be false alarms

questions.hint: With a low base rate, false positives can outnumber true cases.

questions.prompt: "We interviewed ten managers of top-performing teams and all hold weekly meetings, so weekly meetings make teams perform well." What is the main flaw?

options.text: Meetings take time away from other work
Ten managers is too few to tell us anything
It does not check whether weaker teams also hold weekly meetings
Managers may not be honest about their meetings

questions.hint: Selecting on success cannot show what causes success.

items.title: L9: Applying defined terms precisely
items.source: Civil Service online tests: practice guidance, GOV.UK and Civil Service Jobs
items.body: Policies, contracts and legislation define terms, and the definition may differ from everyday meaning. In these questions, the definition in the passage governs. Method: first, pick out the definition and mark its conditions, noting whether they are joined by 'and' or 'or'. Second, apply each to the facts. Third, check dates, counts and thresholds precisely. Fourth, do not import outside knowledge that conflicts with the definition. For example, if a 'dependant' must be financially supported by a household member, a full-time student who gets no financial support is not a dependant under that definition, even though he is under 21 and in education. If 'working day' excludes weekends and public holidays, count only the qualifying days, starting after the day of the event, and skip the holiday. A 'small organisation' that needs fewer than 50 employees and either turnover under £10m or a balance sheet under £5m can qualify on the balance sheet alone. A breach is serious if it affected more than 100 people or involved special category data, so a breach of 80 people involving health data is serious. Fraud requires deliberate dishonesty, so an overpayment made because a claimant did not know about a duty is not on that fact alone fraud. A vulnerable customer may be so temporarily. A repeat complaint must be raised within a stated period after closure, so an interval just beyond it falls outside the rule.

questions.prompt: "A 'dependant' is a person under 18, or under 21 if in full-time education, who lives with and is financially supported by a household member." Ben, 19, lives with his parents and studies full time but receives no financial support from them. Which outcome follows?

options.text: He is not a dependant, because he is over 18
He is not a dependant, because he is not financially supported
He is a dependant, because he lives with his parents
He is a dependant, because he is under 21 and studying full time

questions.hint: All parts of the definition must be met.

questions.prompt: "A 'working day' is any day other than a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday. Appeals must be lodged within 10 working days after the date of the decision letter." A letter is dated Thursday 2 May, and Monday 6 May is a public holiday. What is the last day for lodging an appeal?

options.text: Friday 17 May
Monday 20 May
Thursday 16 May
Thursday 9 May

questions.hint: Counting starts on Friday 3 May, and 6 May is skipped.

questions.prompt: "A 'small organisation' has fewer than 50 employees and either a turnover under £10m or a balance sheet total under £5m." An organisation has 45 employees, a turnover of £12m and a balance sheet total of £4m. Which outcome follows?

options.text: It cannot be said, because its profit is not given
It is not small, because 45 employees is close to 50
It is not small, because its turnover is over £10m
It is small, with fewer than 50 employees and a balance sheet under £5m

questions.hint: The turnover and balance sheet tests are alternatives.

questions.prompt: "A 'serious breach' is one that affected more than 100 people or involved special category data." A breach affected 80 people and involved health data, which is special category data. Which outcome follows?

options.text: It is a serious breach only if it affected more than 100 people
It cannot be said, because the cause is not given
It is a serious breach, because special category data was involved
It is not a serious breach, because it affected fewer than 100 people

questions.hint: Either condition is enough.

questions.prompt: "A report is due 21 days after the end of each quarter. Quarters end on 31 March, 30 June, 30 September and 31 December." What is the due date for the quarter ending 30 September?

options.text: 21 November
31 October
20 October
21 October

questions.hint: 30 September plus 21 days is 21 October.

questions.prompt: "An overpayment is a payment that exceeds entitlement. Fraud requires deliberate dishonesty." A claimant was overpaid because they did not know they had to report a change of job. Which outcome follows?

options.text: It is fraud, because the claimant did not report the change
It is an overpayment, but these facts do not show fraud
It is neither an overpayment nor fraud
It is fraud, because any overpayment is fraud

questions.hint: Dishonesty is a separate requirement from exceeding entitlement.

questions.prompt: "A vulnerable customer is one who, because of personal circumstances, is especially susceptible to harm. These circumstances may be temporary, for example a recent bereavement." A customer, recently bereaved, is struggling to complete a form. Which outcome follows?

options.text: The customer cannot be vulnerable, because the bereavement is temporary
The customer is vulnerable only if they ask to be treated so
The customer may be treated as vulnerable although it is temporary
The customer is vulnerable only if they have a long-term condition

questions.hint: The definition allows for temporary circumstances.

questions.prompt: "A repeat complaint is a complaint on the same subject by the same person within 12 months of the earlier complaint being closed." A complaint was closed on 15 February 2023, and a new complaint on the same subject was made on 20 February 2024. Which outcome follows?

options.text: It is not a repeat complaint, because it came more than 12 months after closure
It is a repeat complaint, because it came within 12 months of the first complaint being made
It is a repeat complaint, because it concerns the same subject
It cannot be said, because the outcome of the first complaint is not given

questions.hint: 12 months from 15 February 2023 ends on 15 February 2024.

items.title: L9: Leading change and handling resistance
items.source: Civil Service Code and Civil Service Leadership Statement, GOV.UK
items.body: The Civil Service Leadership Statement sets out values and behaviours for leaders: setting direction, engaging people, being open, and building trust. When you lead a change, such as a new process or a restructure, people may resist, and the reasons deserve attention before the resistance is judged. Good practice is to explain why the change is needed and what it means for people, listen to concerns and use them to improve the plan, involve people who will use the new process, give training and time, be honest about what is not yet decided, and track the effect. Legal duties apply: where changes affect terms and conditions or jobs, the department must consult properly and follow its policies and any agreements with trade unions. A change should not be pushed through by concealing facts, or by treating those who object as disloyal. Equally, leaders should not drop a well-founded change at the first complaint. The Code also asks for objectivity: use evidence about how the change is working, including bad news. Worked example: staff say the new system makes their work slower. You collect data and examples, share them with the project team, agree fixes, and tell staff what is changing as a result. You do not insist that they are wrong, or silently let them work around the system.

questions.prompt: You are introducing a new case-management system, and several experienced staff say it is slower than the old one. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the most vocal critics to explain their concerns to the whole team
Gather timing data, share it with the project team, and tell staff what will change
Allow staff to carry on with the old system until the complaints stop
Tell staff the system has been chosen at a higher level and they must use it

questions.hint: Evidence-based listening improves the change and keeps trust.

questions.prompt: You are about to announce a restructure, and some of the details are not settled. What is the most effective approach?

options.text: Wait to announce anything until every detail is settled
Share the full details with senior managers only, and let them brief the teams
Explain what is decided, what is not, and when staff will know more
Announce a firm plan and change it quietly later if needed

questions.hint: Honesty about uncertainty builds more trust than silence or false certainty.

questions.prompt: A restructure would change some staff's working hours and locations. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Check the consultation rules with HR and follow them before announcing decisions
Introduce the changes on a trial basis to avoid the formal process
Agree the changes informally with staff you trust, then present them to all
Announce the changes and invite comments afterwards

questions.hint: Changes to terms and conditions require proper consultation.

questions.prompt: A respected team member publicly says the change is a mistake in a team meeting. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them the decision is final and the meeting is not the place to question it
Say nothing in the meeting and avoid them for a while
Ask the rest of the team whether they agree with the criticism
Thank them for raising it, ask for specifics and follow up with them separately

questions.hint: Treating objections as input helps to improve the plan.

questions.prompt: Early data show the change is helping in one office but not in another. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Look into why the offices differ, share both results and adjust
Pause the whole programme until the second office catches up
Report only the successful office's results to senior managers
Apply the same approach to the second office with greater pressure

questions.hint: Objective reporting, including bad news, helps the change to work.

questions.prompt: A colleague suggests presenting a weak business case for the change more favourably, as ministers will otherwise cancel it. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Present the benefits and risks in a balanced way
Suggest speaking to the sponsor about how to improve the proposal
Agree to emphasise the benefits and leave out the main risks
Tell the colleague the case must be accurate and offer to strengthen it honestly

questions.hint: Misrepresenting a business case breaches honesty and objectivity.

questions.prompt: Staff morale has dropped since the change, and some team members seem anxious. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Hold a social event to lift spirits and say nothing more about the change itself
Listen, acknowledge concerns, give clear information and offer support
Ask HR to deal with anyone who seems anxious about the change
Tell staff that morale will improve once they get used to the change

questions.hint: People need information and support, not reassurance alone.

questions.prompt: A union representative raises concerns about how the change affects some staff. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Avoid meeting them until HR has prepared a full written response
Say that consultation will take place once the plan has been finalised
Ask staff to speak to you directly and not through the representative
Meet them, listen and take their points into account within the framework

questions.hint: Engaging with representatives is part of good and lawful practice.

questions.prompt: Several months in, the change is delivering less than promised. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell your manager and stakeholders what you have learned and propose changes
Stop the change and return to the old process without informing anyone
Highlight the small improvements and say nothing about the shortfall
Keep running it quietly and hope the results improve over time

questions.hint: Being open about shortfalls supports good decisions.

items.title: L9: Bullying, conflict and dignity at work
items.source: Civil Service Code, Equality Act 2010 and ACAS guidance
items.body: Civil service departments have dignity at work policies, and the Civil Service Code requires respect for colleagues. Bullying is generally understood as offensive, intimidating, malicious or insulting behaviour, or an abuse of power, that undermines or humiliates a person. Harassment related to a protected characteristic is unlawful under the Equality Act 2010. Not all conflict is bullying: a robust disagreement about work, or a manager giving fair feedback, is not bullying, though how it is done matters. When you witness or hear about poor behaviour, you should take it seriously, avoid taking sides before the facts are known, and use the department's procedures. Informal resolution is often the first step, such as a calm conversation or mediation, but formal routes are needed for serious or repeated behaviour, or if the informal approach fails or is unsafe. Confidentiality should be kept, apart from the people who need to know. Managers have a duty to act when they know about a problem, and cannot ignore it just because nobody has complained formally. Retaliation against someone who raises a concern is not acceptable. Worked example: a team member says a colleague belittles them in meetings. You listen, record what is said, talk to the colleague about the behaviour and its impact, and offer mediation or the formal route if it continues.

questions.prompt: A team member tells you privately that a colleague regularly belittles them in meetings. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Raise it in the next team meeting so everyone hears the standard expected
Tell them to be more resilient and to avoid the colleague
Listen, record what they say, explain the options and speak to the colleague
Wait until the team member makes a formal complaint before acting

questions.hint: Managers must act on what they know, and begin with the options.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues disagree strongly about how to run a project, and the argument is getting personal. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Let them settle it between themselves, as this is a normal difference of opinion
Meet them together to refocus, set ground rules and agree who decides
Take the project away from both of them and give it to someone else
Meet each privately and agree with each of them to keep things calm

questions.hint: Early, balanced intervention resolves conflict and keeps the work moving.

questions.prompt: A new starter says a manager has made comments about their accent that made them uncomfortable. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Suggest they ignore it until their probation period has finished, to be safe
Tell them the manager means no harm and probably did not realise the effect
Speak to the manager informally and then tell the new starter it is resolved
Take it seriously, explain the formal and informal routes and support them

questions.hint: Comments related to race or origin can be harassment, and need proper handling.

questions.prompt: You are told that a manager in another team is shouting at staff, but you have not seen it. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask other colleagues in that team whether the story is actually true
Encourage the person to raise it, and tell them how you can help, using the policy
Go and tell the manager what you have heard about their behaviour
Say you cannot get involved as it is not your team

questions.hint: Supporting people to use the proper route is more effective than investigating alone.

questions.prompt: You are accused by a team member of bullying after you gave them critical feedback on poor work. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask colleagues to confirm that your feedback was reasonable and fair
Withdraw the feedback and apologise to avoid the dispute
Tell the team member they are being oversensitive
Take the concern seriously, tell your manager what happened and engage with the process

questions.hint: Fair feedback is not bullying, but the concern should be addressed openly.

questions.prompt: After a colleague raised a formal complaint, the person they complained about starts leaving them out of meetings. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Do nothing, as the formal process is already dealing with the original complaint
Report the exclusion to the manager or HR as possible retaliation
Record what you have seen and when
Speak to the person about the behaviour and its effect

questions.hint: Retaliation is a separate matter and must be dealt with.

questions.prompt: Mediation was tried between two colleagues, but the behaviour has not changed. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask them to try mediation again without any other changes
Move one of them to another team to avoid further trouble
Consider the formal procedure with HR support and explain to both people
Accept that they will never get on and plan around it

questions.hint: If informal approaches fail, formal steps may be needed.

questions.prompt: A member of staff you manage asks that you do not tell anyone about what they have said about a senior colleague's behaviour. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Report it straight away to HR without telling them first
Promise confidentiality, as they will not speak to you again otherwise
Tell them to talk to the senior colleague directly about it
Explain what you can and cannot keep confidential, and agree next steps

questions.hint: Confidentiality has limits, and being clear is fair to the person.

questions.prompt: In a stressful week, a colleague snaps at you in front of others. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Snap back so that the colleague realises how it feels
Ask whether anything is wrong and if they need help
Let it go if it is a one-off, but raise it if it recurs
Speak to them calmly afterwards about how it affected you

questions.hint: Retaliating escalates the conflict and breaches the behaviour expected.

items.title: L9: Advice under uncertainty and recording decisions
items.source: The Civil Service Code and Managing Public Money, GOV.UK
items.body: Senior officials often give advice when evidence is incomplete and time is short. The Civil Service Code requires advice to be honest, objective and based on evidence, while being clear about what is not known. Good advice sets out the options, the risks, the costs and benefits, the quality of the evidence, and a recommendation, and flags any legal, financial or propriety concerns. Where there is a significant concern, the accounting officer may ask for a written ministerial direction, which means the decision is on the record and may be shared with the Public Accounts Committee. Decisions and the reasons for them should be recorded, as records support accountability, the audit trail and later learning. If new evidence arrives after a decision, you should tell decision-makers promptly, not hold it back. If time is very short, you can give a rapid assessment with its limits, but you should not present an uncertain view as certain. Risks should not be hidden to make an option look better, and benefits should not be overstated. Worked example: ministers want a decision within two days and the evidence is weak. You set out what is known and unknown, the risks of each option, a recommendation and what could be done to reduce uncertainty, and you record the advice and decision.

questions.prompt: Ministers want a decision within two days, and the evidence on the options is thin. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give a short note with no detail on uncertainty to keep it simple
Set out options and risks, state what is uncertain, recommend and record it
Ask for more time without giving any interim advice
Present the strongest option as the clear choice to save time

questions.hint: Honest advice includes the limits of the evidence.

questions.prompt: New data arrives that suggests your earlier advice was too optimistic, after ministers have decided. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Use the data to prepare a defence of the original advice
Mention it only if ministers ask about progress
Tell your manager and the decision-makers promptly and explain what has changed
Wait to see if the data is confirmed by the next release

questions.hint: New evidence needs to reach decision-makers quickly.

questions.prompt: The accounting officer has doubts about the value for money of a ministerial decision. What is the most effective course of action?

options.text: Set out concerns in writing and ask for a written direction if the minister proceeds
Say nothing, as the minister is accountable for policy
Refuse to take any part in carrying out the decision
Tell the press about the concerns to put pressure on the minister

questions.hint: A written direction puts the concern and the decision on the record.

questions.prompt: A manager asks you to tidy up the record of a meeting so that the disagreement about the decision does not appear. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Keep the full version for yourself and give the manager the tidied one
Leave the record unwritten to avoid any argument
Remove the disagreement, as the final decision is what counts
Explain that the record must reflect what happened, and offer fair wording

questions.hint: Accurate records are essential for accountability.

questions.prompt: You have been asked to give a view on the likely cost of a programme, but the estimate depends on uncertain assumptions. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give a single figure that is the most likely, with no explanation
Decline to give any figure until the assumptions are certain
Give a range, state the assumptions and what would change the estimate
Give the lowest figure so that the programme is approved

questions.hint: A range with assumptions is honest and useful.

questions.prompt: A senior colleague tells you not to include a significant legal risk in a submission, because it would complicate the decision. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Take advice from the legal team on how to present it
Leave it out of the submission, as the senior colleague has decided what goes in
Explain that the risk must be included and offer to present it clearly
Raise the issue with a more senior manager if it is not resolved

questions.hint: Significant risks cannot be omitted from advice for convenience.

questions.prompt: You are asked to give oral advice in a meeting, with no time for a written note. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Give your advice clearly, then follow up with a written note of what was decided
Give only a general view to avoid being held to it later
Decline to advise without a written submission
Give the advice and rely on others to remember it

questions.hint: Decisions and advice should be recorded.

questions.prompt: A minister's decision turns out not to have worked as intended, and you are asked who advised it. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Say the advice was sound and that circumstances changed
Say you cannot recall the details of the advice that was given
Give an honest account of the advice given and the evidence at the time
Emphasise that the advice was only one of several views offered

questions.hint: Accountability depends on honest accounts of what was advised.

questions.prompt: You are asked to describe the likely benefits of a policy and can see that the department's own modelling gives a lower figure than the one ministers have quoted. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Use the higher figure, as ministers have already quoted it
Tell the minister's office about the difference and explain each figure
Use the lower figure without mentioning the difference
Present both figures and not say which is better supported

questions.hint: Material differences must be flagged, with evidence and reasoning.

items.title: L9: Grants, partners and public accountability
items.source: Managing Public Money and Government Grants Standards, GOV.UK
items.body: When government funds organisations outside the Civil Service, such as charities, local bodies or suppliers, it must be able to show that public money was used properly. Grants are given for a purpose through a fair process, with published criteria, a clear assessment, and conditions for how money may be used. Government grant standards expect proportionate controls, monitoring and the ability to recover money that is misused. The principles of Managing Public Money, regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility, apply. Civil servants administering grants must be impartial, declare conflicts of interest with applicants, avoid giving some applicants information that others lack, and keep records of decisions and reasons. Fraud and error are reported and followed up. Partners must be treated fairly, and oversight should be proportionate: tight enough to protect public money, but not so heavy that it stops good work. If a partner is struggling, being honest and supportive is better than hiding the problem or abandoning them without notice. Worked example: you find a grant recipient has spent money on something outside the agreed purpose. You do not ignore it or accuse them without checking. You gather the facts, tell your manager and the grants or counter-fraud team, and follow the agreed process.

questions.prompt: You find that a grant recipient has used part of the funding for an activity outside the agreed purpose. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ignore it, since the amount is small and the charity is doing good work
Tell other funders about it before speaking to the recipient
Tell the charity to repay the money immediately without further checks
Gather the facts, tell your manager and the grants team, and follow the process

questions.hint: Misuse of public funds needs proper, fair follow-up.

questions.prompt: A charity you know well is applying for a grant, and a trustee is a friend of yours. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Assess the application as usual, since your friendship is not with the charity
Tell the trustee not to mention the friendship to anyone
Assess it, but score it more strictly to avoid bias
Declare the relationship to your manager and step back from the assessment

questions.hint: Personal relationships create a conflict that must be declared.

questions.prompt: An applicant asks for informal advice on how to improve their bid before the deadline, but no similar help has been offered to others. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Direct them to the published guidance, and offer help only if open to all
Give them tips by phone, since they are well-meaning and new to bidding
Refuse any contact and not reply to their query
Give them a draft of a successful application as an example

questions.hint: Applicants must be treated equally, with information shared equally.

questions.prompt: A partner organisation tells you it is struggling to meet its targets and may need more time. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Tell them to meet the targets, as the conditions are clear
Discuss the problems openly and agree any changes through the formal process
Say nothing to your manager so the partner does not get into trouble
Agree to extend the deadline informally to avoid conflict

questions.hint: Open, supportive engagement within the rules is best for the partner and the public.

questions.prompt: A manager asks you to approve a grant payment, but the recipient has not provided the evidence required under the conditions. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Mark the evidence as received so the payment can be released
Pay half now and the rest when the evidence arrives
Explain that the evidence is a condition and ask for it before paying
Pay the grant and ask for the evidence afterwards

questions.hint: Payment conditions protect public money, and records must be accurate.

questions.prompt: You suspect that a recipient's accounts contain invented invoices. Which response is the least effective?

options.text: Pass your concerns and evidence to the counter-fraud team
Contact the recipient yourself and warn them that you are checking the invoices
Tell your manager and record what you have seen
Avoid any further payments until advised by the right team

questions.hint: Alerting a suspect may allow evidence to be destroyed.

questions.prompt: A minister's office asks you to speed up a grant to a charity in the minister's constituency. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the charity to apply for a different fund
Delay the application until the minister's office stops asking
Fast-track the grant, since the minister's office has asked
Explain that the application goes through the normal process, and tell your manager

questions.hint: Grant decisions must follow the published criteria and not be influenced by connections.

questions.prompt: Monitoring a large grant, you find the controls you were told to apply are very heavy for a small community group. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Ask the group to find a bigger organisation to take the grant
Apply the controls anyway and say nothing
Raise it with your manager and discuss whether lighter controls would still protect funds
Reduce the checks yourself to make it easier for the group

questions.hint: Controls should be proportionate, and changes need to be agreed.

questions.prompt: Two applicants have equal scores for the last place in a funding round, and one has a stronger relationship with your team. What is the most effective response?

options.text: Apply the tie-break in the published criteria, and record your reasons
Fund both, and take the money from other grants
Choose the applicant that your team knows best, as they are more reliable
Toss a coin and not record how the decision was reached

questions.hint: Decisions must follow the stated criteria and be recorded.
